newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends little changed in U.S. after losses pared.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends little changed in U.S. after losses pared.

text.p: The dollar ended mixed in U.S. trade after recovering most of the ground it surrendered overnight.

Dealers said investors had initially misread the statements from a Saturday meeting of the Group of Seven (G7) nations that included a veiled threat to halt the dollar's rally if it continued unchecked.
"After the early volatility, we thought (the selloff) could continue, but it hasn't developed that way. The market would still like to buy dollars, said Vincent Amaru, a vice president at Citibank.
But after a spate of panic selling in Far East trading, the dollar gradually trimmed its losses as bargain-hunters emerged and investors reexamined the statements from the G7 summit in Berlin.
The official G7 statement stated that currency market "misalignments" noted in April 1995 had been corrected and labelled excess volatility "undesirable."
The group also pledged cooperation and stated that economic fundamentals should determine currency market rates.
Market players at first interpreted those statements as a call for an end to the dollar's sharp gains in recent weeks.
"The communique basically stated that the G7 will intervene if the dollar accelerates too quickly or too high," said Amaru. "It would be smart not to test the central banks right away."

In Far East trade, the dollar quickly fell toward 120 yen 1.64 German marks. But by Monday's close, the dollar had rebounded to 122.75/80 yen, up marginally from 122.67/72 at the open, and 1.6560/65 marks up from 1.6540/45 at the open.
Dealers said the market had overreacted to the G7 statement, allowing investors to pick up dollars on the cheap.
Yet many dealers said they now see an inevitable confrontation between dollar bulls and monetary authorities in coming weeks.

"I think (the central banks) will knock the dollar down again," said Perman. "They are not going to let the rise be as rapid if it continues. If the dollar gets back toward 124 or 125 yen, people will be a little cautious."
The dollar has soared more than 50 percent from a post-World War II low 79.75 yen in April 1995, and more than seven percent in 1997 alone.
Should G7 officials opt to sell dollars for yen, dealers expect the initial reaction would be a sharp dollar decline below 120 and possibly further.
"The Bank of Japan has such huge dollar reserves that if they ever wanted to hold it down, they could," Perman said.

In other trade, the dollar edged higher to 1.4255/60 Swiss francs from 1.4235/45 at the open and up from a session low at 1.4155. Sterling rose to $1.6423/33 from $1.6328/38. The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3550/55 from C$1.3515/20.
The Australian dollar rose to $0.7580/85 from $0.7576/81.
